- Inference: When asking whether a player's mechanics are "breaking down" late in a session, compare to that player's own baseline rather than a team norm. The talk says the model differs by athlete (sidearm versus overhand) [20:58]; for football this is a quarterback or kicker session, not a roster rule.
- Inference: Write the injury cost of a key player down for the program in games and snaps. The talk shows one lost player changing a teammate's output (17 sacks to six with more snaps) [10:46], a framing useful when making the case to a coach for load management.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: force-plate reporting follows Output, Driver, Strategy and an optional symmetry group (L/R differences). The talk agrees that landing asymmetry matters but gives no thresholds, so it adds a motivation, not a method.
- Eric's baseline: modified reactive strength index from daily CMJ replaced subjective wellness surveys because it was objective and actionable, and surveys were kept for return to play. The talk's Golden State daily questionnaire [06:43] conflicts with the roster-wide drop, but is consistent with keeping surveys in return to play.
- Eric's baseline: injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, and no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric. The talk asks whether risk can be "avoided" [09:16], a stronger framing; the baseline would treat it as reduce-and-monitor.
- Eric's baseline: the department tracks GPS with Catapult (player load, max velocity, distance). The talk names wearables vendors including Catapult [04:39] without metrics, so no further link.

## What would have to be true

- Baylor force-plate landing or jump tests are run in a repeatable way, so a left/right difference reflects the athlete and not set-up.
- There is enough history per athlete (a pre-injury baseline) to say what asymmetry is normal for that player.
- Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance agree who acts on an asymmetry flag and what the action is.

## Do not apply when

- Treating the DNA, sweat patch and EEG items as usable now. The speaker calls these research-stage and declines to say whether DNA predicts injury [16:55].
- Using the Warriors, Ravens or Kawhi stories as evidence. They are single cases told by a consulting speaker, and he notes other reasons the Ravens went five and 11 [11:16].
- Reading the NBA, MLB and NFL dollar figures as a cost model for a college program [11:16]; they are 2013 pro salary and game-missed totals.
- A sample too small to separate a person's normal from a deficit, such as one athlete with a single session.

## First step

Pull last season's CMJ or landing data for one position group's returning players with a prior lower-body injury and list their left/right difference beside their own earlier values. Read-only, no change to testing.

# Applications: Sport science, extending the athlete's peak performance

## Where this applies

- Inference: Tie one monitored variable to a performance outcome the coaches already care about, and show it in one slide at the start of a session. A panelist did this by linking team sleep totals to passing accuracy [48:31]; at Baylor the pair could be sleep or mRSI against a practice efficiency or PFF-graded measure, shown to the position group.
- Inference: Try a "fluid" week for a small group: keep the planned load but let the player's daily readiness shift the dose up as well as down. The Kentucky example adjusted by 20 to 25% above plan on good days [19:51]. At Baylor this means a rule in the plan, agreed with the strength coach, for when the day goes up.
- Inference: Reframe reports to football coaches so "risk flag" always comes with a modifiable factor and a training change, not only a reduction. A panelist argues that pulling athletes back stops overload [21:22].
- Inference: Replace "wear the device or else" with an explanation of what each athlete gets out of it, and ask players for one reason they would opt out. The panel treats being rejected as personal, not about the science [47:30], and warns against policing athletes [34:10].
- Inference: For nutrition at football scale, start with training-table options and education before individual tracking, as the Kentucky coach did with 120 players [53:07].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: "Recovery has to be earned by training hard first," and heavy load monitoring bred a "culture of fear" of under-training. The panel agrees strongly: recovery is part of adaptation [14:14], and sport science has gone too far toward pulling athletes back [20:22].
- Eric's baseline: the Applied Performance roster-wide wellness surveys were dropped because athletes learned to game them. The panel agrees on the mechanism, saying athletes may say they feel fine to avoid being benched [17:19], and extends it: trust is the fix, not a new metric.
- Eric's baseline: daily mRSI from CMJ was chosen as the objective readiness marker. The panel conflicts in part: it says the best current tool is asking the athlete, and no single number captures recovery [16:47].
- Eric's baseline: preparedness (long-built capacity) is separate from readiness (day to day). The panel's talent versus readiness point, a freshman with low work capacity [18:20], extends this to coach communication.
- Eric's baseline: an annual plan is a flexible roadmap, and the course teaches undulating periodization. The fluid periodization report [19:51] agrees and adds a daily adjustment rule.
- Eric's baseline: the data dictionary has no position-specific thresholds. The panel's point that published thresholds do not hold for real athletes [23:54] supports building them from Baylor data.
- Eric's baseline: NordBord was dropped for 120+ athletes because collection could not be sustained. The panel's note that monitoring every player's food at that size is not feasible [53:07] runs parallel.

## What would have to be true

- Enough weeks of consistent data per athlete to show whether a link such as sleep to performance exists in Baylor's group, not only in one cited team.
- Strength and position coaches willing to agree in advance on the upward-adjust rule and who decides.
- A way to record whether a player chose to opt out of a measure, so opt-outs can be tracked without penalty.

## Do not apply when

- Reading the "150 to like 500%" improvement figure as a result. It is a panelist's recall of a dissertation, no sample or design was given [19:51].
- Acting on the sleep story [30:03] as an effect size. It is one player in one week with a game grade, and the speaker lost the game that week.
- Using the belief-effect findings to withhold real sleep or load data from athletes. They argue for care in how results are framed [22:52], not for hiding them.
- Applying the NBA poster finding on back-to-backs [38:19] to football; it is a basketball injury set the speaker calls limited.
- Applying the 76ers or rugby examples when the coach and athlete group are different: a panelist warns against importing "what worked here" [08:08].

## First step

Pick one outcome a football position coach already tracks and one variable Applied Performance already collects, and plot the two for a single position group across last season. Read-only, and show it to that coach before deciding anything.

---
type: video-summary
video_id: WvLqr1cEso4
title: "SSAC16: Biometrics: The Next (And Biggest) Analytics Frontier"
event: SSAC16 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Andy glockner (caption spelling)]
topics: [basketball, sports-science, injury-health, policy, competitive-advantage]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A media talk (no slides) by the co-founder of The Cauldron, drawn from his new book on how the NBA uses technology and analytics. He argues that biometric and health data is now where on-court analytics was five or six years earlier. He treats keeping players healthy as the most protectable edge, because a rival can see a playing style but not how a team keeps players on the floor. His main concern is not the technology but data ownership, privacy and what players should give up in the coming collective bargaining talks. He also flags known error in tracking data.

## Key claims

- Biometric ideas are not new: diet changes by one star, and a team being fined for resting players in 2012, came before resting became fashionable. [01:39]
- A Warriors assistant general manager said that having two named players healthy for 75 games would tell him all he needed about the team. [02:40]
- A 2013-14 Spurs rotation outproduced peers at every slot, and strategic rest produced no drop-off in performance. [03:42] [04:13]
- Health and rest strategy is the most protectable secret, because a team's draft and playing style can be dissected but its method of keeping players healthy is hard to see. [05:14] [05:44]
- A quoted bioethics attorney says employer control of employee health care is a conflict of interest, and monitoring aimed at predicting performance is an economic purpose rather than a health one. [06:46]
- The reopened collective bargaining agreement is where this fight will be settled, and a cynic reads monitoring as a team benefit. [07:16] [07:46]
- Tools are improving but how to apply, collect and interpret the data on human actors is unresolved. [09:18] [09:48]
- Raw tracking data has an established error rate, including misidentified players and plays. [10:18] [10:48]
- Players cannot wear tracking devices in games until the agreement is reopened, so teams use practice and camera-based data to approximate load and fatigue. [11:18] [11:49]
- A Marquette program was said to be using wearables in college this year. [12:19]
- Who owns testing data (the testing company, the player, the team as employer) is unsettled; agents want it but may not want teams to have equal access. [12:49] [14:24] [14:54]
- The speaker says the larger question is ethics and privacy law, not technical limits. [15:56]
- The players union faces the problem of deciding what to give up while the technology and its uses keep changing. [16:26]
- Teams adopt what other teams adopt, and no one is sure of efficacy yet; some teams ask for raw data without a plan or staff to use it. [17:27] [17:57] [18:27]
- Teams should look for small actionable steps, such as rest and sleep, where the speaker says there is evidence (days of rest, travel). [18:57] [19:27]
- Flexibility loss across a game and then travel is substantial, per the Suns research head. [19:27] [19:58]

## Numbers and definitions

- Raw data error "as much as 15 to 20%" for play differentiation on court, told to the speaker by team personnel; he does not know the figure for force, speed or power. [10:48]
- Dietary change by one star in 2008 and 2009; Spurs resting fine in 2012. [01:39]
- Warriors condition: two named players healthy for 75 games; one played 77 games and the other 67; the team went 83 and 20 (caption wording "83 and 20", likely 83 wins including playoffs, not stated). [02:40] [03:10]
- Dean Oliver's book is dated 2002 or 2003 (caption "2002 2003"). [08:47]
- Season labels such as "20145" and "20134" are caption garbles (likely 2014-15 and 2013-14). [01:09] [03:10]
- A "7,000" injury reports remark is a joke, not a count. [15:24]
- Flexibility: the Suns research head estimates 25% lost across a game and another 10 to 15% after a flight. [19:27] [19:58]
- Adoption timeline for the union answer: next 6 to 12 to 18 months; "six to 12 months" for the story. [17:27] [20:29]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Interpolation: teams combine practice wearable data, off-court training and camera tracking data to estimate game load and fatigue because in-game wearables are barred. [11:49]
- Baseline testing at a pre-draft combine (P3, caption spelling "p 3") and independent testing by the Suns research head. [12:49] [13:21]
- No model, algorithm or formal evaluation is described.

## Limits and open questions

- A media perspective; the speaker also promotes his book. [00:38] [20:29]
- The rookie-class injury story is told without numbers, and he says no player-level prediction was given to him. [13:53]
- The 15 to 20% error comes from unnamed team personnel and refers to basketball camera data, not wearables. [10:48]
- The speaker says no one is sure of efficacy of the data. [17:57]
- Spurs rest and the Warriors anecdote support a view; no controls or sample are shown.
- Names are caption garbled in several places (writers, the Dallas performance director, Suns research head).

## Q&A

None on the recording; the speaker offers to take a few questions privately. [20:29]
=== END ===

type: video-summary

title: "SSAC16: Putting the Data Science into Sport Science"
event: SSAC16 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ray Hensburgger (caption spelling)]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, basketball, american-football, other-sport:baseball, decision-making]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A consulting-firm speaker argues that sports science is moving out of the TV lab and onto fields and courts, with wearables, camera tracking and practice data, and that its current focus is injury. He uses team and player cases (Golden State rest, a pass-rushing duo losing a player, Kawhi Leonard's rehab) to show value, then looks ahead to biochemistry, brain signals and markerless motion capture. His thesis is that technology, people and an iterative data science process must be combined; no single solution fits all, and it does not replace scouts or coaches.

## Key claims

- The speaker's firm is a management and technology consultancy that says it is bringing military-grade data science methods into sport. [00:31] [03:07]
- Sports science means understanding the athlete across body, biochemistry, DNA and mental makeup, to optimize health, performance and game strategy. [04:08]
- Wearables from several vendors, plus NBA, MLB and NFL tracking, now let teams link practice data to in-game data. [04:39] [05:40] [06:12]
- Golden State used a daily questionnaire, tracking data and practice wearable data; red flags after a road trip led the head coach to bench stars. [06:43] [07:14] [07:44] [08:15]
- Sports science is currently focused on injury, especially soft tissue (ACL, Achilles). [08:46] [09:16]
- A lost star affects teammates and results, shown by the Ravens pass-rush case. [10:16] [10:46] [11:16]
- Injuries carry financial costs. [11:16]
- Leonard's rehab used sports science to work on left/right balance, which the speaker credits as part of his MVP-level season. [12:18] [13:51] [14:51] [15:22]
- Plate data on landing can show an athlete favoring one side, and the habit can lead to injury or weakness. [13:20] [13:51]
- Next steps named: DNA, sweat and saliva sensing, brain signals (EEG), and markerless motion capture. [16:55] [17:25] [17:57] [19:28]
- Motion data could show when a pitcher's mechanics break down rather than relying on a pitch count, and the model differs by athlete. [20:28] [20:58]
- Fine measurement such as an elbow drop of three versus three and a half inches may matter for some players and not others. [21:29]
- Technology only generates data; the right data, the right technology and the right people are needed, and the process is iterative rather than replacing people. [22:02] [22:32]

## Numbers and definitions

- Firm size: about 22,000 people, about 600 in the analytics group. [00:31]
- Speaker tenure: 11 years. [02:35]
- Warriors: six game, nine-day road trip; they had 51 wins at the point of benching; a fan tweet cites $250 tickets. [07:14] [08:15]
- Achilles tear: probably at least 14 months for most athletes. [09:46]
- Ravens duo: 29 sacks in 2014, four and a half more than any other duo; one player had 17 of those, then six the next year with 189 more snaps; the Ravens finished "five and 11" (speaker says "I think"). [10:16] [10:46] [11:16]
- The second Achilles tear in that player's career is stated. [10:16]
- 2013: MLB teams spent $665 million on salaries of injured players and replacements; NBA teams lost $358 million; NFL starters missed around 1,600 games. [11:16]
- Leonard: signed for 18 games in his second season with quadriceps tendinitis in 2012 (caption "signed for 18 games", likely a garble of sidelined). [13:51]
- Leonard: 6'7 and wingspan 7 foot three inches; the hand size is joked about and not measured. [13:51] [14:21]
- Pitch count reference: 100. [20:28]
- Elbow drop examples: three inches versus three and a half. [21:29]
- The speaker's own comparison, "best sack duo", relies on that one season. [10:16]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Match practice wearable data to in-game tracking data, and layer athlete baselines on both. [06:43] [20:58]
- Force plates for landing and jump asymmetry. [13:20]
- Overlaying an athlete's mechanics on an ideal using cameras and data. [15:22]
- Markerless motion capture (camera-based, no markers). [19:58]
- The data science process: build predictive models and use machine learning on what is learned, iteratively, with people making decisions. [22:32]

## Summary

A moderated panel (presented by Catapult) of a football high performance coach, a 76ers research head, a rugby and Australian sport veteran, a science writer and a Catapult executive. The theme is that sport science fails when it ignores people: buy-in, trust and culture matter more than any single metric. Panelists argue for individualized load, recovery as part of adaptation, caution against over-reading risk data and against pulling athletes back, and tying measures to performance outcomes players care about. The close covers nutrition monitoring, doping incentives and whether players trust wearables.
